title: High Resolution Hyperspectral Quantum Infrared Imaging with Undetected Photons
authors: Aadi Suketu Bharatia, Vidya Prakash Muppalla, Ananya Asthana, Priyanka Kandankel, Tanmoy Chakraborty, Sreelaja Nair, Anshuman Kumar
abstract: Quantum sensing in the infrared regime often demands the use of expensive and cryogenically operated detectors. Nonlinear interferometry has paved the way for information transfer from the infrared to the near--infrared or visible regime in various quantum technologies. A particularly interesting application of these interferometers involves spectrally--resolved quantum imaging using undetected photons, enabled by the use of temperature--tunable parametric amplifiers. In this work, we demonstrate spectrally resolved transmission imaging with undetected photons around 1550 nm using a spontaneous parametric down conversion based folded nonlinear interferometric scheme, registering the attenuation of a zebrafish larva as a biological feasibility test. We characterize and calibrate the interferometer, having achieved spectrally resolved interference fringes with a maximum baseline visibility of $\sim 74\%$ in the near--infrared regime. Phase--stepped readout of a grating spectrometer gives a resolving power of $\sim1460$ (from the spectrometer's point spread function) at 1550 nm, and $\sim 730$ from the coherence length, the finest reported for imaging with undetected photons, over an instantaneous spectral window of $\approx 51$ cm$^{-1}$.
summary: This paper presents a method for high-resolution hyperspectral quantum infrared imaging by utilizing nonlinear interferometry and undetected photons generated via SPDC. By mapping the object's transmission spectrum onto the visibility of near-infrared photons, the technique avoids the use of costly cryogenic detectors. The successful demonstration on a zebrafish larva proves its potential for label-free biological sensing.
main_problem: The goal is to achieve high-resolution hyperspectral quantum infrared imaging, especially for biological samples, while circumventing the need for expensive, cryogenically-cooled detectors.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated spectrally resolved transmission imaging using undetected photons on an intact zebrafish larva, confirming the technique's biological feasibility.
method: The technique relies on nonlinear interferometry, specifically using a spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) based folded scheme to transfer spectral information from the infrared to the near-infrared/visible regime.
model_or_system: The system uses SPDC in a PPLN crystal, generating signal and idler photon pairs. The measurement maps the object's transmission spectrum via the visibility of the signal photons, which are never directly detected.
key_observables: Spectrally resolved interference fringes, baseline visibility (up to $\sim 74\%$), and spectral resolution ($\sim 730$ from coherence length).
important_parameters: Operating in the single-pair regime ($\mu < 3.7 	imes 10^{-6}$), and the spectral window of $\approx 51 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$.
main_assumptions: The theoretical derivation assumes signal and idler photons are generated into single-modes, and the spatial resolution is currently limited by the idler beam waist.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the experimental setup involving various optical components (DMs, lenses, filters) for the folded nonlinear interferometer.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical framework involving induced coherence and the measured rate equations, followed by experimental characterization of the interferometer, and finally, the application to biological imaging.
why_interesting: This work represents an advanced application of quantum optics and nonlinear spectroscopy to bio-imaging, demonstrating label-free, non-destructive measurement techniques using quantum correlations.
